title: How Black women powered Democratic wins in Mississippi and across the South
content: Jacqueline Amos remembers being on the phone with her father years ago navigating the backroads of Mississippi in an effort to register voters when she drove past a Ku Klux Klan rally. As she watched provisional ballots get counted in Hinds County on Wednesday, with Democrat Scott Colom on the precipice of making history, Amos wished her father were alive to see it. Amos was part of a network of Black women across the state that propelled group chats into on-the-ground momentum and became a visible force for the Colom campaign and turnout operation, from hosting get-out-the vote events to going county by county with a clipboard to register voters. “You get at the table, you get in the room, and everyone did, all of the women. They did the heavy work. But you know, we’ve always done the heavy work,” Amos told CNN. “There were GOTV parties, you know, where folks hosted people in their homes, in their beauty salons, and their personal businesses, and they just had gatherings, and they just continued to get people involved.” On Wednesday, more than a week after the election, that work paid off. Colom became the first Black person elected to the Senate from Mississippi since the Reconstruction era and the first Democrat since 1982. Black women played a major role in Colom’s victory. They made up 20% of the electorate in Mississippi, compared to 5% nationally, according to CNN’s Voter Poll, and Colom won 99% of their votes. When an online commenter asked about the other 1%, Colom joked that it was a “statistical error.” Across the South, Black women voters helped usher in a slew of new Democratic officeholders this year, powering Keisha Lance Bottoms to a history-making win as Georgia’s first Black governor alongside a slate of Black women who will hold key state offices. They also backed successful Democratic candidates in GOP strongholds, including South Carolina and Texas , by lopsided margins. “Mississippi is not a fluke. The new political battleground for America is the South,” LaTosha Brown, a longtime voting rights activist and co-founder of Black Voters Matter, told CNN. “There is no path to the presidency that does not come to the South.” In his victory speech at the historically Black Tougaloo College on Wednesday, Colom honored civil rights icon and Mississippian Fannie Lou Hamer while crediting the women in his life and the ones he met through the campaign. “As my mom would always tell me, faith without works is dead, and we worked this election, y’all,” he said, during a celebration supercharged with excitement and a deep acknowledgement of history. Three Black women who attend a regular breakfast club that Colom visited couldn’t contain their enthusiasm. Students of Tougaloo made a spirit line for attendees to dance their way to their seats. To kick off the event, the Tougaloo choir sang, “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” a hymn known as the Black national anthem, and when Sam Cooke’s “A Change is Going to Come” came on, the crowd joined in. “I’ve seen some strange things happen in my lifetime, and thankfully this is one of them,” Jackson businesswoman Toni Cooley said ahead of Colom’s remarks. “I probably didn’t think that I would see it.” South Carolina’s leadoff position in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary will only amplify the role of African Americans, who make up about a quarter of the state’s population, giving them an early role in shaping a wide-open contest. South Carolina Democratic Party Chairwoman Christale Spain, the first Black woman to lead the state party, said the midterm results reinforce the importance of her state holding the Democrats’ first presidential primary. “As we look toward 2028, any potential Democratic presidential nominee must recognize the importance of these voters and be willing to understand their priorities and concerns,” Spain said in statement. “Black voices must continue to be part of the conversation here and throughout the South if we want to see this level of success again.” Dyamone White was at a dinner with Colom in Chicago at the Democratic National Convention in 2024 when Colom said he was going to run and noticed quickly that the party wasn’t taking Colom’s race seriously. White said she was used to losing and voter apathy. But in 2023, White helped organize events for Black women supporting Democrat Brandon Presley’s run for governor. While Presley ultimately lost by three points, White started to notice a shift in voter engagement that she helped capitalize on to support Colom’s campaign. “We learned then how to make Black women connect to policy,” White said. Now, she has a message for everyone who had written Mississippi off: “Wake up and smell the coffee.” In Jackson, Patricia Smith, a longtime Democrat, was not going to be deterred. Even though she was a regular voter, she told CNN that when she showed up to vote on Election Day for Colom she was told she wasn’t listed in the poll book and had to fill out an affidavit ballot. Somehow, she said, the system had her listed at an address that she hadn’t lived at since 1991. Smith was one of thousands of Mississippians who cast provisional ballots because they were not included in precinct poll books or did not have appropriate photo identification. But Smith’s vote was saved. A fellow Black woman who was working as an observer watching officials sort through affidavit ballots gave Smith a call as soon as she recognized her name. “What it does for me is renews my faith. That, and I don’t mean to sound churchy with this, but God has not forgotten us,” she said. Cassandra Welchlin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women’s Roundtable, said the group registered about 600 new voters this year as part of its “Power of the Sister Vote” campaign. It organized a massive post-election tele-townhall to coach voters on how to correct problems with provisional ballots. “This moment really speaks to the courage, the actions, the fortitude and the determination of Black women,” Welchlin said. Colom’s wife, Nadia, who was been instrumental in strategizing how to mobilize young voters and Black women, spoke to her daughters from the stage Wednesday night with a reminder of their motto: “Colom girls never quit.” Strategists point to a “Blacklash” that built across the region in response to both the inflationary pain felt by a growing number of Americans and the GOP’s aggressive moves in the last year to curb Black political power. The Supreme Court’s gutting what remained of the power to bring claims of racial discrimination under the 1965 Voting Rights Act in response to redistricting loomed large. Within days of the court’s decision in Louisiana vs. Callais, Republican-controlled legislatures in Tennessee , Louisiana and Alabama raced to carve up congressional districts with substantial Black populations. “Black voters were feeling like they’ve been getting beat up on and attacked and like their rights were threatened and decided that they were that they were ready to fight back,” said Terrance Woodbury , the president of Democratic research firm HIT Strategies. Anneshia Hardy, a voting rights activist in Alabama, said the Callais decision provided a “tangible example” of threats to Black representation that in the past have sometimes seemed more abstract to voters. “They weren’t just voting for a party, they were voting for survival,” Hardy said. In Alabama, Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures won reelection after the state’s post-Callais redistricting forced him into a district that Trump would have won by 14 percentage points in 2024. Figures previously told CNN the Black voting-age population in the district dropped from 47% to 40% under the new map. On Election Day, he still won by nearly eight points. “That meant something,” Hardy said.” “That in itself kept folks’ political imagination intact.” In Louisiana, Black voters — particularly Black women — helped Democrat Jamie Davis come within 2 percentage points of winning the state’s Senate race against Rep. Julia Letlow. The grandson of a sharecropper, Davis would have become Louisiana’s first Black senator ever. Davis is now weighing whether to challenge Republican Gov. Jeff Landry, who is up for reelection in November 2027. “I think it sent a really powerful message to our elected leaders here at the state level as we go into statewide elections in ’27,” said Ashley Shelton, who runs the Power Coalition, a group that works to build political power for people of color in Louisiana. Two Black female Democrats are also in runoffs next month for House seats in Louisiana. The districts lean Republican, but Shelton said the candidates — state Rep. Pat Moore and Chauna Banks, a former East Baton Rouge Metro Council member, have “viable paths.” “There’s a lot to be work done, but it’s a question about are voters going to show back up and I think they will,” Shelton said. Black voters, she added, “absolutely can decide the runoff.” Even though Georgia did not redraw its congressional map after the Callais decision, the fallout from the ruling still stirred Black voters there, according to one Democratic organizer. Eelise Davis, who was a regional organizing director for Georgia Democrats’ coordinated campaign, said the ruling came as voters in one of her counties, majority-Black Macon-Bibb County, were already concerned about the closure of some longtime polling sites. “Once the redistricting was happening in other states and then polling locations suddenly start disappearing, they’re like, ‘Wait, what’s going on?’” Davis said. “That was definitely the fear.” The day after Democrats romped in the midterms in Georgia, flipping the state House, outgoing GOP Gov. Brian Kemp announced he would not call a special legislative session this year on redistricting while his party still retained power of both chambers. “The voters of our state have spoken,” he said in a statement.
ranking_reason: Black women's role in Democratic wins in Mississippi and across the South is a significant political development.

analysis.reason: Black women's role in Democratic wins in Mississippi and across the South is a significant political development.

final_quality.reason: The article reports a significant political development, highlighting the crucial role of Black women in Democratic wins in Mississippi and across the South, which is a meaningful newsworthy topic.

title: What we know about Brooklyn building collapse that killed eight people
content:
Eight people have died and 18 more were injured after a three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood of Brooklyn, New York.
Witnesses described hearing a loud boom and seeing dust in the air as the building came down and fell into an adjacent construction pit where people were working on Wednesday.
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, described a harrowing scene, saying workers "who had only barely survived themselves turned back and dug victims out of the rubble".
The city's fire commissioner, Lillian Bonsignore, said firefighters were on the scene within minutes and called their actions "incredibly heroic".
Rescue operations ended about 24 hours later on Thursday after fire officials determined there were no more victims at the site.
The site, which had been hit by hard rain and falling temperatures, has been turned over to the Department of Buildings and the New York police.
The building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn was constructed in the 1930s. It contained apartments and a store.
At the construction site next door, plans have been approved for a new building that will include 64 residential units and a grocery store on the bottom floor.
Active work was happening on the site, and it appears part of the building fell into the construction pit, trapping and killing some workers.
It is too early to say what caused the building to collapse at around 16:00 local time (21:00 GMT) on Wednesday, but officials say they are looking into the possibility of filing criminal charges.
The structure was fully occupied by residents, and construction workers were performing excavation work on a neighbouring site at the time, according to CBS News, the BBC's US partner.
It's not clear if the construction had anything to do with the collapse, and the city's buildings department says it is still investigating.
Investigators have said developers have active permits for excavation and foundation work associated with the new building project. The developer has been identified as Robert Fischman.
In a post on X, Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said: "We are working closely with the Department of Buildings and our law enforcement partners to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy."
Mayor Mamdani later emphasised this message in a news conference, saying that every entity involved in the building and the construction site will be investigated, and held accountable.
Eight people - six adults and two children - were killed, authorities said. Two were construction workers.
A further 18 people were injured.
Mamdani said that six people were pronounced dead at the scene, while another two died in hospital.
Four of the injured are firefighters. One person still in hospital is in a critical condition.
A senior official with the NYPD identified the victims  as Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9, Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31, Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10, Barry Mamadou, 23, and Ndiaye Mamadou, 31, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner. They were residents of the building that collapsed.

title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
content:
Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment.
"People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC.
After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter.
"Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion.
Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next."
Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.
But within less than two weeks, federal forces marched triumphantly into Mekelle. The TPLF made what it called a "strategic withdrawal" from the city and Tigray's other main towns so the army encountered little resistance. Hundreds of people are reported to have died in the conflict, including dozens killed by drone strikes and bombing raids by the air force.
Ethiopian government officials and supporters argue that the war is effectively over and that the only remaining task is to clear Tigray of TPLF elements.
Getachew Reda, a senior TPLF official who switched sides and is now an adviser to the prime minister, declared that the war in Tigray had ended and that stabilising the region should now be the immediate priority.
Cameroon Hudson, an analyst and consultant on African peace and security, says there are various reasons for the TPLF's rapid defeat.
"The TPLF has lost popular support at home. It is fragmented, it does not possess the advanced military technology necessary to match the ENDF [Ethiopian National Defence Forces]," he says. "It has lost many of its generals, strategic thinkers, finest diplomats and fighters, either through defections or arrests. The infighting within the TPLF leadership has caused significant damage."
Abraha Hailezgi, a scholar at Mekelle University, agrees. "The army lacks a clear political vision. In recent years, it has become associated with coercion, abuses, forced recruitment and arbitrary actions. As a result, many people have come to view the TPLF army as an adversary rather than a force acting on their behalf," he says.
Speaking by telephone from an undisclosed location, TPLF spokesperson Mikael Asgedom denies that the group has lost.
Instead, he describes it as a deliberate tactical and strategic retreat. "This is not a defeat," he tells the BBC.
He says the TPLF "intentionally allowed the ENDF to advance deeper into the heartland of Tigray", where it can be isolated and confronted on favourable terrain. "We chose not to fight on terms favourable to the enemy."
The TPLF is preparing for a major counteroffensive, he says, adding that TPLF fighters have launched attacks against Ethiopian forces in several locations following their withdrawal from the region's towns, arguing that these operations demonstrated the group's continued military capability.
It is hard to get verified information from Tigray and the BBC is unable to report from there. But phone lines and the internet, which were cut when fighting broke out, have now been restored.
Residents in different parts of Tigray tell the BBC that fighting is continuing in central, northern and north-western parts of Tigray, with the use of heavy artillery and drone strikes.
Eyewitnesses around Sheraro, a town near the Eritrean border, report heavy fighting involving artillery and ground forces in recent days.
"We could hear heavy artillery fire from the Sheraro direction. People are concerned because there is no sense of security," a businessman tells the BBC on condition of anonymity. He adds that military convoys from both sides had moved towards Sheraro, while a motorcycle operator in the southern town of Yechila says military checkpoints are still active.

analysis.reason: Conflict in Tigray region of Ethiopia has significant human consequences

final_quality.reason: This article reports a significant and timely development in the ongoing conflict in Tigray, providing a human interest angle and insights from key stakeholders. The piece provides a clear reason for readers to care, as it sheds light on the humanitarian situation and the implications of the conflict's outcome for the region and its people.
